Multiplying each row in the first matrix by each column in the second, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1\cdot 0+0\cdot (-1) & 1\cdot 1+0\cdot 2 \\ -5\cdot 0+1\cdot (-1) & -5\cdot 1+1\cdot 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}BA & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0\cdot 1+1\cdot (-5) & 0\cdot 0+1\cdot 1 \\ -1\cdot 1+2\cdot (-5) & -1\cdot 0+2\cdot 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ -11 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** Notice that 

$$
AB \neq BA.
$$

Matrix multiplication is not **commutative**, meaning that when we switch the order of multiplication, we often get a different result (like we did in this example).
